sections.b: 2 Chronicles 1–9 tells Solomon's reign as one long act of building and worship. He seeks the LORD at Gibeon and receives wisdom and wealth (1:1–17), builds the Temple with Hiram's help (2–4), brings in the ark and prays the prayer of dedication (5–7), sets the priests and Levites in their places (8:12–16), and is visited by the queen of Sheba (9). Chronicles leaves out the struggle for the throne (1 Kings 1–2), the judgment of the two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28) and, most strikingly, his foreign wives, his idols and God's anger at him (1 Kings 11:1–40). Scholars explain the silence in several ways: an idealized reign joined to David's as one golden age, readers assumed to know Kings, or a theology that would have required telling his punishment too. The book does let a hint through: the people complain of the heavy yoke Solomon laid on them (10:4).

sections.b: Chronicles retells the building of the Temple with the tabernacle always in view. The site is Mount Moriah, the threshing floor where David's altar stood (3:1). The craftsman is a Danite's son like Bezalel's partner Oholiab (2:14), and the furnishings include the bronze altar and the priests' courtyard (4:1; 4:9). At the dedication the Levites lift the ark, the singers praise, and a cloud fills the house (5:4; 5:13–14). Then fire falls on the altar as at the tabernacle (7:1; Leviticus 9:24). Solomon's letter to Hiram and his prayer both insist that no house can contain God (2:6; 6:18), and God's answer names the Temple a house of sacrifice and of prayer (7:12–16).

sections.b: In 2 Chronicles 5 the ark completes the journey begun in 1 Chronicles 13 and 15. As David had ruled, the Levites lift it (5:4; 1 Chronicles 15:2), and it is placed beneath the cherubim's wings with its poles still in it, holding only the two tablets from Horeb (5:7–10). Solomon's prayer closes with Psalm 132's call, "up, LORD God, to your place of rest" (6:41). The ark is mentioned again in Chronicles only when Josiah tells the Levites to put it back in the house (35:3).

sections.b: Chronicles tells Solomon's request at Gibeon more briefly than Kings: he asks for "wisdom and knowledge" to lead and judge the people (1:10), a pairing drawn from the language of the wise. It leaves out the judgment of the two mothers, so the proof of his wisdom comes in his building and in the queen of Sheba's visit (9:1–8). Hiram praises God for giving David "a wise son" who will build the house (2:12), so wisdom in Chronicles is above all the skill to build God's house and order its worship.

Chronicles copies the visit from 1 Kings 10 almost word for word. The small differences are telling: the queen says God set Solomon "on his own throne, as king for the LORD your God" (9:8), where Kings says "on Israel's throne," and she sees the stairway by which he went up to the LORD's house (9:4), where Kings has his burnt offerings. In Chronicles the visit is the last great scene of Solomon's life, not the prelude to his fall.

Chronicles spells the king's name Huram and tells the treaty from Solomon's side: Solomon writes first, asks for timber and a craftsman, and explains the purpose of the Temple (2:3–10). Hiram's reply praises "the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth" (2:12). Chronicles leaves out the twenty towns Solomon gave Hiram, which Hiram disliked (1 Kings 9:11–13), and says instead that Solomon rebuilt the towns Hiram had given him (8:2). Hiram's sailors join Solomon's on the voyages to Ophir and Tarshish (8:18; 9:21).

2 Chronicles 1–12 shows the Chronicler's methods clearly. Some chapters are near copies of Kings (5; 6; 9; 10), and on this site they use the same English wherever the Hebrew matches. Others reshape Kings: Gibeon becomes the place of Moses' tent (1:3–6), the treaty with Hiram is rewritten from Solomon's side (2), and the towns given to Hiram become towns received from him (8:2). Some material is new: the Levites' music at the dedication (5:11–13), the fire from heaven and God's promise of 7:14, Rehoboam's fortresses and family (11:5–23), and Shemaiah's preaching during Shishak's invasion (12:5–8). And whole chapters of Kings are left out: Solomon's sins (1 Kings 11) and the history of Jeroboam's kingdom (1 Kings 12:25–14:20).

sections.b: Chronicles keeps Solomon's prayer from 1 Kings 8 almost whole, adds that he knelt on a bronze platform in the courtyard (6:13), and ends it with Psalm 132 instead of the exodus (6:41–42). God's reply adds a promise not found in Kings: "and my people, over whom my name has been called, humble themselves and pray, seeking my face and turning back from their evil ways, then I myself will hear from the heavens" (7:14). The rest of 2 Chronicles tests that promise king by king, starting with Rehoboam (12:6–7).

sections.h: Cloud and fire at the dedication
sections.b: Chronicles tells of God's glory filling the Temple twice. First a cloud fills the house as the singers praise, so the priests cannot serve (5:13–14), as in 1 Kings 8:10–11. Then, when Solomon finishes praying, fire falls from heaven on the offerings and the glory fills the house again (7:1–3), which Kings does not report. The scene recalls the tabernacle, where the glory filled the tent and fire came out to consume the offering (Exodus 40:34–35; Leviticus 9:23–24).

2 Chronicles 3:1 is the only verse that calls the Temple's hill "Mount Moriah," linking it with "the land of Moriah" where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2). It also names it as the threshing floor of Ornan, where David's offering stopped the plague (1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1). Jewish tradition built on the link, and the Temple Mount is still called Moriah. Many scholars think the identification is the Chronicler's own; the Samaritans located Abraham's mountain on Mount Gerizim.

sections.h: The threshing floor becomes the Temple
sections.b: 2 Chronicles 3:1 places the Temple at "the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite," the place David bought and where fire from heaven answered his offering (1 Chronicles 21:26). The fire falls again on Solomon's altar there (7:1), linking the two scenes.

Chronicles adds the Levitical singers to the story of the dedication. They stand east of the altar, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun with their families, dressed in fine linen with cymbals, harps and lyres, beside a hundred and twenty priests with trumpets (5:12). The cloud of glory comes as they sing, "For he is good, for his loyal love is forever" (5:13), and the same refrain is sung when the fire falls (7:3; 7:6). Solomon then sets the Levites at their posts by David's order (8:14).

sections.b: Chronicles explains why Solomon worshiped at the high place of Gibeon: Moses' tent of meeting and Bezalel's bronze altar were there (1:3–6), while the ark was in David's tent in Jerusalem (1:4). The same arrangement is described in 1 Chronicles 16:39–40 and 21:29. The large site at el-Jib north of Jerusalem has been identified as Gibeon by inscribed jar handles.

2 Chronicles 4:2–6 describes the Sea as in 1 Kings 7:23–26, with three differences: oxen instead of gourds under the rim, 3,000 baths instead of 2,000, and an explanation of its purpose, "The Sea, though, was where the priests washed" (4:6), like the bronze basin of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:17–21).

Chronicles copies the story of the split from 1 Kings 12 (2 Chronicles 10), but then follows only Judah. It never tells of Jeroboam's coronation or his reign, except where they touch Judah. It still treats the north as part of Israel: Shemaiah calls them "your kinsmen" (11:4), the faithful from every tribe come to Jerusalem to seek the LORD (11:16), and later kings will invite the north back (13:4–12; 30:6–9).

Chronicles mentions Jeroboam's rise only in passing (9:29; 10:2; 10:15) and never tells of Ahijah's torn cloak. Its main addition is what Jeroboam did to the Levites: he threw them out of their work as priests and set up priests of his own for the high places, the goat idols and the calves (11:14–15), so the Levites came south to Jerusalem. Abijah's speech will condemn the same priesthood (13:8–9).

Chronicles turns the short report of 1 Kings 14:25–28 into a lesson. It gives Shishak 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen and troops from Libya, the Sukkites and Cush (12:3), says he took Judah's fortified towns (12:4), and explains the invasion: "because they had acted unfaithfully toward the LORD" (12:2). When the leaders humble themselves, God spares Jerusalem from destruction but leaves Judah to serve Shishak for a time (12:5–8).

Chronicles gives Rehoboam three chapters. Chapter 10 follows Kings. Chapter 11 is new: Rehoboam obeys Shemaiah and does not fight the north (11:1–4), builds a ring of fifteen fortified towns (11:5–12), welcomes the Levites and the faithful from the north (11:13–17), and has a large family, naming Abijah, Maacah's son, as heir (11:18–23). Chapter 12 shows the turn: once strong, he leaves the LORD's law, Shishak invades, and when he humbles himself he is spared, though Chronicles' verdict is that "he did evil" because "he had not made his heart ready to seek the LORD" (12:14).

common: Rehoboam is remembered as the foolish son who lost most of his father's kingdom by refusing to lighten the people's load.
uncommon: Chronicles credits Rehoboam with three faithful years and with sparing Jerusalem by humbling himself, so his reign is a mixed picture rather than a simple failure (11:17; 12:12).

sections.b: Chronicles is known for what scholars call immediate retribution: good and bad deeds bring their results within the same lifetime, and often a prophet explains the link. God's reply to Solomon states the principle (7:14; 7:17–22). Rehoboam's reign is the first example: three faithful years bring strength (11:17), leaving the LORD brings Shishak (12:1–2), and humbling brings rescue (12:6–7; 12:12). Critical scholars (Wellhausen, Japhet) read this as a theology the Chronicler imposed on his sources. Others (Dillard, Williamson) stress that it is not mechanical: repentance can change the outcome, and the pattern is a call to return rather than a ledger.

common: God always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life.
uncommon: In Chronicles the pattern is mainly a call to repent: almost every punishment comes with a warning or a way back, as with Rehoboam (12:5–8).

claude.title: Claude's theory: retribution as preaching
claude.body: My own view: Chronicles' pattern is best read as preaching to its first readers rather than as a theory of how the world always works. A small community after the exile, told that their own generation's choices mattered and that God would answer their humbling, would hear in Rehoboam not a formula but an invitation. Even its harshest verdicts usually come after a prophet's warning, as Shemaiah's does (12:5).

sections.h: The promise to David in Solomon's prayer
sections.b: Solomon's prayer twice asks God to keep his word to David (6:15–17), and in Chronicles the prayer ends with a plea from Psalm 132: "Remember the loyal love shown to David your servant" (6:42). God's answer restates the promise as "A man of yours will never be cut off from ruling over Israel" (7:18), where Kings has "from Israel's throne," a wording some scholars connect with Micah 5:2.

sections.b: Chronicles' version of Solomon's blessing has a line missing from Kings: God chose no city and no man before, "But I chose Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I chose David" (6:5–6). God's reply confirms it: "This place I have chosen for myself, to be a house of sacrifice" (7:12). Rehoboam's summary repeats the phrase: Jerusalem is "the city the LORD chose from all the tribes of Israel as the place to set his name" (12:13).

sections.h: Priests and Levites under Solomon and Rehoboam
sections.b: Chronicles gives the Levites a larger role than Kings. They lift the ark (5:4), sing at the dedication (5:12), stand at their stations with David's instruments (7:6), and are set at their posts with the gatekeepers by David's order (8:14). After the split the priests and Levites of the north leave their lands and come to Judah, because Jeroboam has replaced them with his own priests (11:13–15).

Two verbs for seeking, darash and biqqesh, run through this stretch. Solomon and the assembly "sought" the bronze altar at Gibeon (1:5, darash); God promises to answer those who humble themselves and seek his face (7:14, biqqesh); the faithful of the north come south "to seek the LORD, the God of Israel" (11:16, biqqesh); and Rehoboam's reign is judged because "He had not made his heart ready to seek the LORD" (12:14, darash).

The word Chronicles uses most for repentance is "humble oneself" (nikhna). God first uses it in his answer to Solomon (7:14). Rehoboam and Judah's leaders are the first to do it, and God spares them: "They have humbled themselves, so I will not destroy them" (12:7). The same verb marks the turning of Hezekiah and Manasseh, and Josiah later.
